issues.item: Threat: Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
issues.explanation: For trauma to a loved one, nocturnal checking for one's own immediate physical safety is not impossible, but paired with the rest of the profile it introduces a more direct personal-danger threat theme that is not otherwise represented in triggers or memory. The triggers and memory items are centered on reminders of the loved one's trauma/loss rather than the patient's own current physical danger, so this specific item is the least coherent threat item.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am
issues.explanation: Self-blame based on one's character can occur after a loved one's trauma, but here it sits awkwardly beside appraisals focused on institutional failure and lack of accountability, which externalize blame to others. This is not impossible, but this item is the most internally tensioned within the appraisal node and less clearly linked to the rest of the profile than guilt on recall would be.

vignette: Ahmad is a 52-year-old Middle Eastern man who has been widowed for several years. His life took an unimaginable turn when his wife was caught in crossfire during a public event. Despite the chaos and urgency of the moment, Ahmad was unable to reach her in time. He recalls the scene vividly; it is as if he can see every detail, from the panicked faces of onlookers to the sound of sirens approaching. The incident has left him with fragmented memories that do not fit together cohesively, and each time he remembers the event, intense guilt overwhelms him. Since the traumatic event, Ahmad's life has been marked by a series of maladaptive strategies and avoidance behaviors. He often goes along with whatever others want to feel safe-a form of people-pleasing that has become a habit. This tendency is especially evident in his work as an actor, where he finds himself agreeing to roles or conditions he would otherwise reject. Ahmad's efforts to avoid being alone have led him to spend more time on set and at auditions than ever before. He fears the solitude of his home, which now feels like a room filled with painful memories. Crowded places such as shopping centers or public events are particularly triggering for Ahmad. The noise and commotion remind him of that fateful day, and he often finds himself withdrawing from social gatherings. His avoidance behaviors have taken a toll on both his personal life and his career. He has missed out on key auditions and networking opportunities because of his fear of crowds, leading to a decline in professional engagements. The auditory triggers are particularly potent for Ahmad. The sound of children crying or any sounds reminiscent of the event can bring back vivid flashbacks that leave him feeling trapped in a cycle of fear, horror, anger, guilt, and shame. These negative emotions are compounded by his belief that even when others tell him he is safe, it is impossible for him to believe them. Ahmad's inability to trust safety contributes to his constant state of hypervigilance. Ahmad has come to believe that the institutions and people who should have protected him let him down. The fact that those responsible have faced no consequences further fuels his sense of injustice and powerlessness. He struggles with a profound inaction guilt, believing he will never forgive himself for not doing more to stop what happened. This guilt is a constant presence, gnawing at him whenever he recalls the event. In recent months, Ahmad has found it increasingly difficult to concentrate on his work and daily tasks. The fragmented memories and persistent negative emotions make it hard for him to focus or engage fully in any activity. His life feels like a series of disconnected moments, each one fraught with anxiety and distress. What finally brought Ahmad to seek help was a particularly severe episode triggered by media coverage of a similar incident. He realized that his avoidance behaviors were no longer sustainable and that he needed professional support to navigate the complex web of emotions and thoughts that had taken over his life. In therapy, Ahmad hopes to find a way to reconcile his fragmented memories, reduce his hypervigilance, and learn coping strategies to manage his guilt and negative beliefs. Despite his fears, Ahmad is most hopeful for a future where he can regain some sense of control and peace. He wants to be able to trust that the world can sometimes be safe again, even if it feels impossible right now. With each passing day, Ahmad holds on to the possibility that through therapy, he might find a path toward healing and acceptance.
